44784717.article_content:
‘I think about the unknowns and how we can make them less unknown’ … Demis Hassabis at Google's London offices.
Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The Guardian
View image in fullscreen
‘I think about the unknowns and how we can make them less unknown’ … Demis Hassabis at Google's London offices.
Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The Guardian
The G2 interview
DeepMind
Interview
Demis Hassabis on our AI future: ‘It’ll be 10 times bigger than the Industrial Revolution – and maybe 10 times faster’
Steve Rose
The head of Google’s DeepMind says artificial intelligence could usher in an era of ‘incredible productivity’ and ‘radical abundance’. But who will it benefit? And why does he wish the tech giants had moved more slowly?
Mon 4 Aug 2025 00.00 EDT
Last modified on Mon 4 Aug 2025 10.40 EDT
Share
I
f you have a mental image of a Nobel prizewinner, Demis Hassabis probably doesn’t fit it. Relatively young (he’s 49), mixed race (his father is Greek-Cypriot, his mother Chinese-Singaporean), state-educated, he didn’t exactly look out of place receiving his medal from the king of Sweden in December, amid a sea of grey-haired men, but it was “very surreal”, he admits. “I’m really bad at enjoying the moment. I’ve won prizes in the past, and I’m always thinking , ‘What’s the next thing?’ But this one was really special. It’s something you dream about as a kid.”
Well, maybe not
you
, but certainly him. Hassabis was marked out as exceptional from a young age – he was a chess prodigy when he was four. Today, arguably, he’s one of the most important people in the world. As head of Google
DeepMind
, the tech giant’s artificial intelligence arm, he’s driving, if not necessarily steering, what promises to be the most significant technological revolution of our lifetimes.
As such, Hassabis finds himself in the position of being both a booster for AI and an apologist for it. The Nobel prize in chemistry was proof of the benefits AI can bring: DeepMind’s AlphaFold database was able to predict the hitherto-unfathomable structures of proteins, the building blocks of life – a breakthrough that could lead to myriad medical advances. At the same time, fears are ever growing about the AI future that
Google
is helping to usher in.
Being an AI ambassador is the part Hassabis didn’t dream about. “If I’d had my way, we would have left it in the lab for longer and done more things like AlphaFold, maybe cured cancer or something like that,” he says. “But it is what it is, and there’s some benefits to that. It’s great that everyone gets to play around with the latest AI and feel for themselves what it’s like. That’s useful for society, actually, to kind of normalise it and adapt to it, and for governments to be discussing it … I guess I have to speak up on, especially, the scientific side of how we should approach this, and think about the unknowns and how we can make them less unknown.”
In person Hassabis is a mix of down-to-earth approachability and polished professionalism. Trim and well groomed, dressed entirely in black, he wears two watches: one a smart watch, the other an analogue dress watch (smart but not too flashy). He gives the impression of someone in a hurry. We’re speaking in his office at DeepMind’s London headquarters. On the walls outside are signed chess boards from greats such as Garry Kasparov, Magnus Carlsen and Judit Polgár. He still plays; there’s a board set up on a table nearby.
View image in fullscreen
Hassabis being awarded the Nobel prize in chemistry by the king of Sweden last year.
Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images
It was the chess that started Hassabis down the path of thinking about thinking. Between the ages of four and 13 he played competitively in England junior teams. “When you do that at such a young age, it’s very formative for the way your brain works. A lot of the way I think is influenced by strategic thinking from chess, and dealing with pressure.”
On paper there’s little else about Hassabis’s background that foretold his future. His family are more on the arty side: “My dad’s just finished composing a musical play in his retirement, which he staged at an arthouse theatre in north London. My sister’s a composer, so I’m kind of the outlier of the family.” They weren’t poor, but not super-wealthy. He moved between various state schools in north London, and was homeschooled for a few years.
He was also a bit of an outsider at school, he says, but he seems to have known exactly where he was going. His childhood heroes were scientific pioneers such as
Alan Turing
and
Richard Feynman
. He spent his chess winnings on early home computers such as the Sinclair ZX Spectrum and a Commodore Amiga, and learned to code. “There were few people that were interested in computers in the late 80s. There was a group of us that used to hack around, making games and other stuff, and then that became my next career after chess.”
In the 90s, the games industry was already working with AI. When he was 17, he coded the hit game

data.title: Ongoing Lean formalization of the proof for Fermat's Last Theorem
data.author: anonyonoor
data.article_summary: Imperial College London正在进行一个开源项目，旨在使用Lean定理证明器形式化费马大定理（Fermat's Last Theorem）的证明。该项目由Kevin Buzzard主导，由EPSRC资助，计划持续到2029年9月。项目采用Richard Taylor和Buzzard讨论后确定的路线，基于Wiles/Taylor-Wiles的现代变体证明。项目信息和贡献指南可在项目的GitHub页面和相关文档中找到，目前已有620个星标和88个分支。该项目托管于Imperial College London，并获得Apache-2.0许可。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕Fermat's Last Theorem在Lean中形式化的讨论，涉及Lean工具、形式化证明方法及相关技术问题。

不同观点：
• [YossarianFrPrez] 认为Lean背后的组织形式是一种新的科研 nonprofit 模式，对创业者或感兴趣于科研的人很有用，并提供了相关资源链接。这一评论更关注科研组织的创新形式，而非技术细节。

• [ants_everywhere] 对使用 Lean 进行形式化证明表示支持，但认为 Lean 在处理 quotient types 时引入了额外的公理作为一种“作弊”手段，使得从数学角度看不够完美。评论者对使用不同语言的优劣进行了比较，暗示可能存在比 Lean 更合适的语言。

• [seanwilson] 提供了有关该项目的详细概述和相关文件链接，帮助其他人了解项目背景和工作量，未对技术细节提出质疑或讨论。

• [mensetmanusman] 关心项目进展的可视化问题，询问是否存在能够展示当前进展的图形化表示，强调了项目进展透明度和可视化的重要性。

• [amelius] 提出是否可以利用 OpenAI 的 IOM 算法将现有的证明直接转换为 Lean 代码，暗示自动化工具可能加速或简化形式化过程。

• [tphyahoo2] 详细讨论了构造性数学与经典逻辑的区别，指出 Wiles 的证明依赖于矛盾证明法，并质疑 Lean 形式化过程中是否会将矛盾证明法转化为构造性证明。评论者关注形式化证明的逻辑基础及其在不同数学体系中的适应性。

补充讨论：
• 争议的焦点之一是使用 Lean 是否是最佳选择，特别是在处理 quotient types 时引入额外公理的做法是否合适。
• 另一个讨论点是形式化证明过程中矛盾证明法的使用及其在 Lean 中的实现方式，涉及到经典逻辑与构造性逻辑的区别。
• 自动化工具（如 OpenAI 的 IOM 算法）在形式化证明中的潜在应用也是一个讨论热点，表明技术进步可能影响未来的形式化工作流程。

An ongoing multi-author open source project to formalise a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in the Lean theorem prover.
Information about the project
The project is currently being led by Kevin Buzzard. Until September 2029 it is being funded by
grant EP/Y022904/1
, awarded by the EPSRC. The project is hosted at Imperial College London. Kevin would like to extend many many thanks to both of these institutions for their ongoing support of this nonstandard research.

here
.

blueprint
.

data.title: Microsoft is open sourcing Windows 11's UI framework
data.author: bundie
data.article_summary: 微软正在计划逐步开放Windows 11用户界面框架WinUI的源代码，但由于其复杂性和与操作系统专有层的关联，无法一蹴而就。微软将分阶段开放WinUI的GitHub仓库：首先增加内部提交的镜像频率，然后允许外部开发者本地构建、提交代码和运行测试，最终使GitHub成为开发和社区互动的主要平台。尽管开放过程需要时间，微软正在积极推进，同时优先考虑安全性、稳定性和现有产品支持。开发者可以通过提供反馈和提交问题来参与贡献。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Windows原生UI技术的未来及相关框架的争议

不同观点：
• paavohtl认为，Windows 11用基于WebView的应用替代原生应用，导致性能下降和视觉不一致，背离了传统上操作系统开发者应展示良好性能和一致性的责任。
• arunc指出，微软以资源分配为由，将框架推给社区，但缺乏真正的善意和长期支持，暗示微软不负责任。
• pjmlp表示，Windows开发社区对WinUI不感兴趣，特别是那些因Windows 8以来多次失败而失望的开发者，认为微软不会解决现有问题。
• muhehe认为，Windows的UI框架繁多且混乱，质疑开源是否真的对开发者有实际好处，还是仅为了表现开放。
• tekdude支持继续开发WPF，认为其具有一定的优势和改进潜力，如编译时代码生成和性能提升，但担忧时间和资源投入问题。

补充讨论：
• LarMachinarum提到，不仅是Windows，跨平台和开源UI框架也存在问题，如GTK的混乱和Qt的许可模式，认为目前缺少一个好的跨平台原生UI框架。
• daemin批评WinUI3的开发体验差，调试麻烦且示例程序崩溃，因此继续使用Win32和WTL。
• Springtime希望Windows 11引入原生垂直任务栏功能，目前依赖第三方工具实现。
• chiph怀念过去微软提供的UI开发支持，认为现代工具缺乏帮助开发者创建与系统无缝集成的应用。
• bob1029偏好使用Win32/GDI/DirectDraw等低级API，认为这些API稳定且不易被微软改变。
• BoorishBears幽默地指出，Windows拥有众多UI框架且各有缺陷，没有明确赢家。
• bobajeff质疑微软为何不直接采用Electron/TypeScript作为Windows UI框架，特别是微软已经拥有GitHub和vscode。
• dehrmann认为，Windows市场份额下降，微软可能对整个Windows平台的投入减少，用户转向其他设备。
• eska提到，单个开发者能通过学习OS和WinAPI创建高性能原生UI，暗示微软应更注重原生开发。
• AraceliHarker认为，微软对WinUI失去兴趣，意图用WebView替代，开源仅是形式。

争议焦点：
• 微软是否对Windows原生UI技术（如WinUI）失去兴趣，转向基于Web的技术。
• 开源框架是否真正对开发者有益，还是仅为微软的战略转移手段。
• Windows平台的未来发展方向及微软的长期投入承诺。

44765600.article_content:
Microsoft has plenty of open-source projects, and these days, the company is much more open to community contributions. Still, plenty of code remains closed-source, and the company constantly receives more requests to open it. One of them is WinUI, Windows 11's user interface framework. While Microsoft is not opening it fully yet, the company shared details about plans for the next six months, which include "product work and foundational changes to support a more open and collaborative future."
Microsoft
says
that open-sourcing WinUI cannot be done with a switch flip due to its complexity and connections. Windows 11's user interface taps into many proprietary layers of the operating system that cannot be published as is. As such, Microsoft needs to separate what could be shared with the community and what cannot.
Many of you have asked about truly open sourcing the repo. While we’re not ready to commit to a specific end date for completing all milestones, we are actively working toward it. This isn’t a flip-the-switch moment, it’s a deliberate process.
Additionally, the team needs to prioritize other things, which include security, stability, and support for existing products.
Microsoft plans to open WinUI's GitHub repository in phases:
Phase 1: Increased Mirror Frequency
. After the WASDK 1.8 release (end of August), we’ll begin more frequent mirroring of internal commits to GitHub to increase transparency and show progress.
Phase 2: 3rd Party Devs Build Locally
. External developers will be able to clone and build the repo locally, with documentation to guide setup and dependencies.
Phase 3: 3rd Party Devs Contribute & Run Tests
. Contributors will be able to submit PRs and run tests locally. We’re working to untangle private dependencies and make test infrastructure publicly accessible.
Phase 4: GitHub as Center of Gravity
. GitHub becomes the primary place for development, issue tracking, and community engagement. Internal mirrors will be phased out.
Making WinUI more open will be an incremental process, and you can track it on
this board on GitHub
. Meanwhile, developers can contribute by sharing their feedback, filing clear and well-written issues, and upvoting existing feedback.

data.title: Remote hosting for your telescope
data.author: gregorvand
data.article_summary: Sierra Remote Observatories (SRO) 提供位于内华达山脉的顶级望远镜 hosting 服务，自2007年起运营，目前有超过174台望远镜。该地点具备卓越的天文观测条件，夏季视宁度1角秒，冬季1.2角秒，峰值可达亚角秒级，每年290个晴夜，黑暗程度21.80 Mag/ArcSec²，平均风速1英里/小时，无夏季季风。基础设施包括24/7技术支持、光纤互联网（1 Gbps，可升级至更高速度）、现场机械修理服务、Starlink备份网络等。提供每月2小时免费技术支持，并可协助安装望远镜。租用价格从每月600美元起，也提供如iTelescope等可租用望远镜选项。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：远程天文台托管服务及其相关话题

不同观点：
• [支持观点] tbagman 推荐了 StarFront Observatories，认为其地理位置优越， skies 条件好，且采用了高密度托管模式，降低了成本，吸引了大量深空天文摄影爱好者。此外，还提到偶尔会有协作项目，提供了更多互动机会。
• [应用场景扩展] fudged71 提出了远程托管模型是否适用于其他非计算领域的疑问，例如3D打印农场，显示出对该模式广泛应用的兴趣。
• [成本质疑] michaeldoron 对所谓的“免费”技术支持提出质疑，指出技术支持实际上是包含在600美元/月的费用中的，属于文字游戏。
• [家庭教育需求] jalk 表达了希望带孩子体验天文观测的愿望，但由于旅行和夜间时间的限制，寻找在线服务（提供导览和“动手”望远镜控制）未果，显示了对用户友好型服务的需求。
• [惊喜发现] teddy-smith 表示对远程天文台托管服务的存在感到高兴，显示出对新技术和体验的开放态度。
• [体验质疑] _xerces_ 对远程服务持怀疑态度，认为这剥夺了人们亲身接触星空和学习天文学的乐趣，质疑其对传统天文爱好的影响。
• [共享经济模式] RainyDayTmrw 提出了时间共享模式的可能性，认为可以多人共享一个望远镜的使用时间，显示出对经济可行性的关注。
• [其他服务推荐] incognito124 提到了另一个位于西班牙的远程望远镜托管服务，提供了更多选择。
• [商业模式赞赏] ge96 提到了YouTube上有人建立了远程操作望远镜的牧场，认为这是一个很酷的商业模式，显示出对创新商业模式的认可。
• [成本敏感] yapyap 认为600美元/月的价格对普通人来说过高，建议普通收入人群更倾向于在自己后院托管望远镜，显示出对成本的敏感性。

补充讨论：
• 评论中提到了多个远程望远镜托管服务的例子，包括StarFront Observatories和Pixelskies Astro，显示出这一市场的多样性和国际化。
• 对远程天文台服务的不同态度反映了传统天文爱好与现代科技结合的争议，尤其是亲身体验与便捷性之间的平衡。
• 对成本的讨论显示出不同收入群体对远程托管服务的接受度差异，以及对经济可行性的关注。

data.title: Facts will not save you – AI, history and Soviet sci-fi
data.author: veqq
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：人工智能（特别是大型语言模型LLM）在历史叙述、翻译和内容创作中的作用与局限

不同观点：
• munificent认为，由于历史叙述本质上是基于选择性事实和主观信念的重构，LLM无法胜任这项工作。科技公司试图用LLM取代这些工作以控制叙事，从而影响世界。
• dale_glass指出，AI的真正风险在于让我们误以为不需要历史学家或翻译人员。这些领域依赖大量日常工作维持，而AI可能消除这些工作，导致领域萎缩，类似于摄影行业从模拟向数字转变时的困境。
• stereolambda提到，许多历史文献并未数字化或在互联网上公开，LLM无法解决这一基础设施问题。同时，历史叙述往往忽略了大部分事实，仅关注某些主要国家的叙事。
• derbOac认同历史叙述中无法做到完全客观，但一些故事和理论经过更严谨的论证和辩护，具有更高的可信度。
• tombert对微软关于AI取代开发人员的说法持怀疑态度，认为展示AI完成简单任务并不足以证明其能处理复杂、长期的项目，并质疑企业宣传AI能力的动机。

补充讨论：
• ping00分享了一篇短篇小说的阅读体验，并询问其他读者推荐的类似风格作品，这与主讨论点稍有偏离。
• fpoling提供了翻译中文化背景缺失的实例，强调人类翻译在理解和传达背景信息方面的重要性。
• pavel_lishin通过个人经历说明翻译中文化背景和语言细微差别的复杂性，指出即使是人类翻译也常有错误，AI在这方面更具挑战。
• Phui3ferubus和Obscurity4340认同翻译工作正被AI取代，因为企业更注重成本而非质量。

争议焦点：
• AI是否能真正替代需要复杂背景知识和主观判断的工作（如历史叙述和高质量翻译）。
• 企业对AI能力的过度宣传及其潜在动机。
• AI对某些职业（如历史学家、翻译人员、开发人员）的实际影响和替代程度。

data.title: I asked four former friends why we stopped speaking (2023)
data.author: mooreds
data.article_summary: 这篇文章讲述了作者在28岁时对友谊的反思和困惑。作者与最亲密的朋友Simone因生活变化而逐渐疏远，同时在搬到肯尼亚后，也难以融入当地社交圈，感到孤独和不安。作者试图通过与过去的朋友对话，了解友谊破裂的原因，但大部分人无法理解她的困境。文章探讨了人在20多岁时因生活转变、恋爱关系和优先级变化而失去朋友的普遍现象，并表达了缺乏友谊的孤独感和对自我价值的怀疑。作者最终决定通过直接对话 former friends，寻找答案和解决办法。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：朋友关系的演变与维持

不同观点：
• TrackerFF认为，朋友关系会随着人生阶段和责任的变化而改变。年轻时由于共同兴趣和环境结交的朋友，可能会因为生活变化（如工作、家庭）而渐行渐远，但随着孩子长大和生活稳定，可能会重新建立联系。
• netsharc幽默地提出了一种应用创意，通过类似"Tinder"的方式来重新连接过去的朋友，但也提到如果没有匹配成功，可以连接心理健康顾问。
• axelpacheco表示，有些朋友即使很久不联系，也不意味着友谊的终结，但意识到这一点可能促使人思考是否需要采取行动。
• avereveard对文章缺乏结论感到不满，并列出了影响友谊持续的因素，如生活转变、缺乏相互努力、价值观分歧等。
• 202508042147分享了与高中朋友断联的经历，认为不再享受彼此的交流时，断开联系反而是一种解脱。
• windowshopping提供了保持友谊的实用建议，包括保持定期沟通、关心对方的生活、适应对方的沟通方式、处理好与对方伴侣的关系、以及创造共同经历。
• silisili引用Matt的故事，强调在20多岁时忙于建立事业和家庭，可能忽略朋友，但随着年龄增长，朋友和亲人变得更加重要。
• programmertote认为，失去与老朋友的联系是生活的一部分，不必感到内疚，人会随着成长而改变，如果缘分到了，可能会再次相遇。
• mmmlinux简短指出，人会改变，环境也会改变，如搬到其他国家。
• ferguess_k描述了因家庭生活而与老朋友渐行渐远，但通过节假日仍保持联系，同时也结交了新朋友。
• malshe感谢Whatsapp帮助保持与老朋友的联系，并在旅行时主动联系。
• jeffhwang赞赏文章作者的坦诚，认为重新连接朋友或公开讨论断联是很难的事情。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点之一是朋友关系的自然演变与人为维持之间的平衡。一些人认为朋友关系会自然变化，不必强求，而另一些人则强调通过努力可以维持友谊。
• 另一个值得注意的讨论点是，技术（如Whatsapp）在维持友谊中的作用，以及如何利用技术有效地保持联系。
• 最后，如何处理与朋友伴侣的关系也被提及，作为维持友谊的一个重要因素。

On a warm July evening, I dove into bed and grabbed my phone, giddy and anxious. As I scrolled through TikTok, attempting to calm my nerves, a Google Calendar notification flashed on the screen: “VIDEO CALL WITH SIMONE.”
Before I could swipe the reminder away, Simone FaceTimed me. I attempted to rehearse my greeting as the call buffered:
Should I keep it cool with a, “Hey, what’s good?” No, that sounds cold. What about a Keke Palmer-esque, “Girl!” No, that’s doing too much. “Good evening?” No, it’s not evening her time, that doesn’t even make sen—
“Girl!” Simone said with a chuckle.
I couldn’t help but crack a smile. As I’d learned over the course of our six-year friendship, her warmth never failed to replace my anxiety with joy.
“Damn, it’s been a
minute
.” she added.
She was right. Though Simone is my closest friend, we don’t see or talk to each other often. Both are my fault. In 2020, after months holed up in my tiny Washington, D.C. apartment, I decided to wait out the winter at my mother’s cottage in Kenya. It was just what the doctor ordered, and a few months later, I decided to move to Nairobi permanently.
My move changed our friendship—it changed
all
of my friendships, actually. I tried to stay in touch with my friends stateside for a while, but as time went on, FaceTime dates became harder to plan, and fewer voice notes were exchanged via WhatsApp. Now, I don’t know if I can call any of them friends anymore—and my relationship with Simone felt like it was hanging by a thread.
Things in Kenya aren’t much better. Though I’m Kenyan by ethnicity, I grew up abroad, in the US and UK, and I’ve found that my foreign accent and perspective other me, even within my family. These days, my social life tends to begin and end with nights on the couch, re-watching
Shameless
with my boyfriend. I’m ashamed and terrified about that reality; it feels dangerous to rely on only him for human connection.
After all, friends are witnesses to your life. They enrich the living experience. Not having that makes me feel like that tree that falls in the forest alone: Can anybody hear me? Do I matter?
Marriage and family therapist Shontel Cargill promises me that these feelings are normal. She says that friendship loss in one’s mid-to-late 20s is common for several reasons: life transitions, romantic relationships, evolution of priorities, and more. And while it doesn’t happen to everyone, for some, friendship loss “can lead to psychological distress,” sparking issues with anxiety, depression, trust, and self-esteem.
Check, check, check, and check.
Cargill says that talking about your struggles with others can help the healing process, but I’ll be honest—that hasn’t worked for me. Most people I’ve spoken to about my predicament don’t get it, which only makes me feel worse. I tried to bring it up on my aforementioned call with Simone, but her empathetic smile and pitying eyes said it all: She couldn’t relate. Lucky her.
I needed answers. Concrete ones—not those generic suggestions that I “put myself out there” or “just give it time.” Everyone around me had managed to hold on to friends throughout their lives; everyone seemed to be on girls’ trips and boozy brunches; seemed to have a tribe of confidants ready to drop everything for them. And here I was, a lonely, overworked 28-year-old who spent way too much time in her apartment, wondering why she didn’t have any of that.
So, like a good journalist, I decided to investigate. After speaking to Simone, I determined that I’d reach out to some of my former friends directly, and see if we could have a conversation about why we “broke up.” Many declined, and understandably so. But to my surprise, a few agreed to participate in my crazy scheme.
Here are those conversations—and their revelations. Their names have been changed.
Celine
Circumstance brought Celine and me together. We were both new freshmen at an international school in Nairobi, and our shared fear proved the perfect BFF elixir. Celine was sweet and reserved, with a quiet confidence that I admired—even more so when I got older. But she wanted to do her own thing and I, a not-so-confident 14-year-old, wanted to fit in. I had a hunger for popularity, and when I realized that Celine didn’t share that, I neglected the friendship. Soon, it evaporated.
Celine remembered things similarly.
“Once school started, we new kids were initially welcomed into the group of ‘misfits’ that every high school has,” she wrote to me via Facebook. “But eventually, we broke away—you, to join the funny kids, a group of hilarious and friendly people who could match your unparalleled wit and high-octane energy and me, to join the kids at the back of the bus, literally and figuratively.”
I thought that by the end of high school, we were strangers. But Celine reminded me that we had our special moments, and that there was always love between the two of us. “By senior year, we were moving in completel

data.title: Show HN: I spent 6 years building a ridiculous wooden pixel display
data.author: benholmen
data.article_summary:
本文讲述了作者花费六年时间打造了一个不实用的1000像素木制显示屏，名为"Kilopixel"。该项目灵感来源于一些非传统艺术作品和低帧率的电子墨水屏播放器，旨在创建一个任何人都能通过网页互动的低效显示器。显示屏采用40x25的像素网格，每个像素通过单一机制逐一旋转，与现代显示器相比效率极低。

作者首先尝试使用木制结构和各种材料作为像素，包括乒乓球、泡沫球、木球等，但由于成本、重量和易碎性等问题均未成功。最终，在2024年，通过与他人讨论，作者决定放弃球形像素，改为使用立方体像素。

项目涉及网络应用、物理控制器、定制CNC构建、3D建模和打印等多方面技术，是作者迄今为止最雄心勃勃的项目。读者可以通过kilopx.com亲自体验这个独特的显示屏。

44787902.article_content:
I spent 6 years building a ridiculous wooden pixel display
August 2, 2025
TL,DR: I built the world's most impractical 1000-pixel display and anyone in the world can draw on it
If you just want to play with it, goto
kilopx.com
.
The backstory
Six years ago I had an idea to build a large, inefficient display with a web interface that anyone could interact with. I've enjoyed
Danny Rozin's unconvenional mirrors
over the years and was inspired by an
eInk movie player that played at 24 frames per
hour
that got me thinking about a laborious display that could slowly assemble an image.
I landed on the idea of a 40Ã25 pixel grid of pixels, turned one by one by a single mechanism. Compared to our modern displays with millions of pixels changing 60 times a second, a wooden display that changes a single pixel 10 times a
minute
is an incredibly inefficient way to create an image. Conveniently, 40Ã25 = 1,000 pixels, leading to the name
Kilopixel
and the six-letter domain name
kilopx.com
. How do you back down from that? That's the best domain name I've ever owned.
So I got to work. This project has everything: a web app, a physical controller, a custom CNC build, generated gcode, tons of fabrication, 3d modeling, 3d printing, material sourcing - so much to get lost in. It's the most ambitious project I've ever built.
The first prototype: 21Ã3 pixels
My first thought was to use a wooden gantry that would ride on some sort of track. Since I'm most comfortable working with wood, it's my default prototyping medium. However, I quickly pivoted to extruded aluminum and the excellent
hardware kits from Openbuilds
that include pulleys, gantry parts, extruded aluminum, and timing belts. It's very similar to the materials used in 3D printer frames, and connects very easily with off the shelf stepper motors. This allowed me to build a gantry with X and Y, essentially a wall-mounted XY plotter. I built the first prototype with two stepper motors, a Raspberry Pi, a CNC controller, and a beefy power supply. It allowed me to generating and sending instructions to the CNC controller to move to a particular pixel, turning that pixel, and reading values from sensors. It also revealed quite a few problems with my pixel choices and pixel manipulation mechanisms.
1,000 of anything is
expensive
Picking pixels was a real adventure. I've tried ping pong balls, styrofoam balls, bouncy balls, wooden balls, 3d printed balls, golf balls, foam balls...anything approximately spherical and about 1-1.5in in diameter. The problems I encountered were largely cost (even a 50Â¢ ball is $500 of balls), weight (again, a thousand of these things), and availability. For a long time I thought ping pong balls were my best bet, so I purchased a few hundred of them, 3d printed painting jigs, and spray painted them. I used a hot nail to melt two opposite holes on each ball so they could be strung up on the display.
Ping pong balls are basically soda cans
You can stand on a soda can,
as long as it's not open
. Open the can, and it crushes easily. Ping pong balls are the same way. They're relatively strong until you melt two holes in them. Then they can be deformed, which is fatal to any spray paint you've put on them. And not only are they fragile, but the cheap ones are inconsistently sized, and a half millimeter here and there adds up when you have a row of 40 balls. Ping pong balls were a no-go.
Nerfed
My next attempt at a cheap, spherical pixel was foam Nerf balls - much smaller than ping pong balls, and only available in bright colors. They accepted spray paint OK but the paint deteriorated over time.
It was difficult to consistently bore a hole through the nerf balls, and they really liked to grab the wire and were hard to turn. I struggled to consistently turn them and I wasn't thrilled with the bright colors.
I also tried bouncy balls (hard to drill a hole, hard to paint, inconsistent sizes, heavy), wooden balls (not very round, hard to paint a crisp line, heavy), and styrofoam balls (hard to paint with acrylic paint, and they melt with spray paint).
Turning balls
I had the idea to use a small, slow motor to rotate a LEGO wheel against the ping pong ball. I'd use a reflectivity sensor to detect if it was showing black or white, and stop once the pixel was rotated properly. I modeled and printed a custom hub for a LEGO wheel, a few different mechanisms to move the wheel in and out of contact of the sphere, and an interface for the gantry. I tried using a solenoid to push the motor into the ball, which was underpowered, and a servo. Neither approach worked great and ultimately I decided this ball turning approach was a dead end.
Pivoting to non-spherical pixels
In 2024 I had a couple of productive conversations with
Joe Tannenbaum on the Side Project podcast
and
Chris Morrell on the Over Engineered podcast
. Those conversations helped me consider that maybe balls were not the way to go - I thought about flaps and illuminated buttons, then settled on a cubic

data.title: Gigabyte removes PCIe 5.0 support from B650 motherboards in latest BIOS update
data.author: josephcsible
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：B650主板对PCIe 5.0支持的问题及相关消费者反应

不同观点：
• Aurornis认为，B650主板从未正式支持GPU插槽的PCIe 5.0，只有B650E主板才支持。他解释说，M.2插槽和扩展插槽在规格上存在区别，B650主板的设计和测试都是基于PCIe 4.0的预期，如果强行启用PCIe 5.0可能会导致不稳定和系统崩溃，增加退货率和顾客不满。

• Amatecha表达了对购买的主板被宣传支持PCIe 5.0但实际仅限于M.2插槽的困惑和不满。他提到自己刚购买的电脑明确标示支持PCIe 5.0，但现在意识到仅限于存储而非GPU插槽，并表示会继续使用当前BIOS版本以避免问题。

• Toast0指出，类似的情形在AM4平台上也曾发生过，暗示这种情况可能是厂商更新或调整产品特性的一部分，而非个例。

• Josephcsible提出，厂商不应在售后收回已售产品的功能，即使该功能存在bug或未被正式宣传。他认为这种做法应被视为非法。

• Oakwhiz从技术角度提出疑问，认为可能是信号完整性问题导致无法支持PCIe 5.0，暗示硬件设计上的限制可能是根本原因。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点在于消费者对产品功能预期的落差以及厂商是否应在售后取消或调整产品特性。
• 部分用户对产品规格的理解存在混淆，特别是M.2插槽和GPU插槽在PCIe支持上的不同。
• 有人提出这种现象并非首次发生，可能与硬件设计和测试的局限性有关。
• 法律和消费者权益问题也被提及，特别是产品功能被“收回”是否合理。

data.title: Show HN: Kimu – Open-Source Video Editor
data.author: robinroy03
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：视频编辑器的功能、性能、用户体验以及市场定位

不同观点：
• [Uehreka] 认为要信任视频编辑器，必须看到其实际处理复杂项目的能力，例如处理多视频文件、效果和内存管理等。他还指出，初学者在编辑时更可能不规范操作，因此编辑器需要能处理未经优化的素材。此外，他建议不要从零开始构建编辑器，而应借鉴成功产品如Cursor，利用现有UX和插件生态。

• [vivzkestrel] 提出了一种语音控制或手势控制的视频编辑器设想，认为这种创新可以摆脱鼠标和键盘的限制，提升用户体验。虽然目前没有这样的编辑器，但他描述了其可能的操作方式。

• [Mr_Eri_Atlov] 分享了简单的使用体验，并建议增加图像居中功能，以便处理不同大小的图像时更方便。

• [ojr] 认为市场上已有许多类似视频编辑器，新产品需要在移动端优先发展，而不是仅限于网页端，并提到Capcut的免费桌面应用是一个强有力的竞争者。

• [xnx] 和 [microflash] 分别询问新编辑器与OmniClip和OpenCut的比较，关注其独特卖点和区别。

• [sitkack] 建议在时间线上预填充正在进行的编辑，以便用户能立即开始体验和操作。

• [leptons] 对即将推出的AI代理功能持怀疑态度，认为不需要因为AI流行而添加，可能会分散开发视频编辑器的核心目标。

补充讨论：
• 初学者与专业编辑者在使用习惯上的差异，以及如何设计编辑器以适应不同用户群体。
• 视频编辑器的市场竞争，尤其是移动端和桌面应用的竞争，以及如何在功能和用户体验上进行差异化。
• 对AI功能的态度，部分用户认为AI功能可能并不必要，甚至会分散编辑器的核心功能开发。

争议焦点：
• 视频编辑器是否应从零开始构建，还是应借鉴现有成功产品的架构和功能。
• AI功能是否对视频编辑器有实际帮助，还是仅为迎合潮流的噱头。

data.title: Lidar-based GIS map of New Hampshire stone walls
data.author: rob
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：新英格兰地区的石墙历史、石墙地图的应用和准确性

不同观点：
• [PyWoody] 指出新英格兰地区的石墙并非如神话所说由霜冻推石而成，而是在大约三十年时间内因养羊业而由人工建造。他引用了Tom Wessels的视频系列来支持这一论点。
• [mikeocool] 补充说明了新英格兰地区石墙的形成背景，由于当地多岩石的土壤，农民将田里的石头移到一旁形成石墙。随着农业的重要性下降和土地的重新造林，这些石墙被遗留下来。

补充讨论：
• [rob] 提供了一个在康涅狄格州查找石墙的LiDAR地图链接，并推荐了具体使用的选项，为实际查找石墙提供了工具。
• [uptime] 提到一些石墙位于百年以前的道路遗迹上，现在这些地方已经被森林覆盖，强调了石墙的历史性和自然环境的变迁。
• [flipnotyk] 从专业角度评论了LiDAR地图的精度，提到其在GIS项目中对数据精确度的要求，对地图的准确性表示赞赏。
• [joshuamcginnis] 提出了对石墙地图实际用途的疑问，引发了对该信息应用价值的讨论。
• [lemonberry] 对地图上街道名称的错误提出了意见，但也确认了地图上一些石墙的准确性。
• [jppope] 从个人兴趣角度出发，表示对石匠技艺的兴趣，认为该地图对学习石工技艺很有帮助。

争议焦点：
• 石墙形成原因的误解与真实历史之间的对比。PyWoody和mikeocool都反驳了关于石墙形成的常见误解，并提供了历史背景和证据支持。

data.title: DrawAFish.com Postmortem
data.author: hallak
data.article_summary: DrawAFish.com 网站经历了一次约6小时的安全事件，期间用户名被恶意篡改为侮辱性词汇，不当的鱼图被批准，正常的鱼图被删除。根本原因包括：遗留的6位管理员密码在过去的数据泄露中被曝光，用户名更新API缺乏身份验证，以及JWT未绑定到特定用户。事件发生后，通过手动恢复管理操作、修复授权逻辑并审查备份来解决问题。此次事件源于作者的快速开发（“vibe-coding”）和多个安全漏洞，如暴露的旧密码和未认证的API。最终，在社区帮助下，问题得以解决，作者从中吸取了教训，强调了高速度开发中的风险。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：关于一个低风险项目“vibe-coded”鱼类展示的评论，涉及安全问题、项目趣味性以及技术细节的讨论。

不同观点：
• [ofjcihen] 认为该项目展示了明显的安全漏洞，但因为项目风险低，觉得其文档记录完整，具有一定的幽默感。同时提到，在处理生产环境中类似问题时，自己的工作负载有所增加。
• [vicdemydov1] 对项目的文档记录表示赞赏，并提到该项目与乐高“建造鱼类”展览的相似性，认为这种互动体验具有成瘾性。
• [amiga386] 以讽刺的口吻指出“vibe-coded”中的“S”应代表“安全”，暗示项目在安全方面的不足。
• [Havoc] 提到有人利用安全漏洞来反击恶意行为，认为这种情况很疯狂。
• [somethingawful2] 担心在热门网站上排名靠前会导致个人信息被曝光（doxxing），并询问这种情况是否常见。
• [dmje] 赞赏项目的写作风格和幽默感，并表示希望看到更多类似内容。
• [davikr] 指出项目中JWT（JSON Web Token）认证机制的问题，即未验证JWT与用户身份的关联性，导致潜在的安全风险。
• [thehamkercat] 提到任何人都可以无需认证给鱼类投票，且每分钟每IP地址限制为20票，指出项目在投票机制上的技术细节。
• [lawlessone] 从用户体验角度建议添加镜像功能，以便更容易绘制面向右的鱼。
• [kergonath] 对项目的趣味性表示赞赏，同时提到希望看到有关破坏行为的截图。
• [comrade1234] 分享了在苏黎世发生的类似破坏行为事件，提到在一幅恐龙壁画上出现不雅涂鸦，引发公众笑声。
• [nullc] 引用经典语句“So long and thanks for all the fish”，表达对项目的赞赏。
• [bmau5] 表示项目非常有趣，希望看到更多类似项目。
• [jmull] 讨论了快速编码和代码审查的重要性，质疑使用LLM（大型语言模型）生成代码的合适性，并引用原作者的观点，即LLM是工具，需要人工审查。
• [ofrzeta] 提到有人可能正在研究让LLM自动提交代码，并对“黑客”如何关联到neopets.com用户账户表示好奇。

补充讨论：
• 项目中的安全问题成为讨论焦点，特别是JWT认证机制的漏洞和投票机制的无需认证问题。
• 项目趣味性和互动体验受到多数评论者的赞赏，但也有人提到破坏行为和不雅涂鸦等负面影响。
• 对LLM生成代码的讨论涉及到代码审查的必要性和快速编码的吸引力。

争议焦点：
• 项目中的安全漏洞和如何有效防范恶意行为是主要争议点。
• 对LLM生成代码的适用性和人工审查的重要性存在不同看法。

44784743.article_content:
DrawAFish.com
TL;DR:
Incident Duration:
~6 hours (2AM–8AM EST)
Impact:
Username vandalism (slurs)
Offensive fish approved / safe fish removed
Root Causes:
Legacy 6-digit admin password exposed in past data breach
Username update API lacked authentication
JWT not tied to specific user
Mitigation:
Manual reversal of mod actions, fixed authorization logic, backups reviewed
Takeaway:
hwoopsy daisy 🙂
Did you see? Did you see it? What it says? What it says on top of the website?
If you were on HackerNews on
Aug 1 2025
, you may have seen
DrawAFish.com
.
Because it was in the number 1 spot. You also may have seen it if you follow me on
instagram
. You also probably saw
that I was in the #1 spot on Hackernews there too. Because I posted about it a lot. And also if you
talked to me in person you probably heard about it. And then you probably heard a lot of quotes from
The Social Network
(2010) where I replaced various words with "Fish."
"A million fish isn't cool. You know what's cool?
A billion fish
."
If you read the post on Hackernews, you saw that the website was an exercise in
vibe-coding. I used Copilot to implement features, and I used it to implement features
fast
.
In my career,
[0]
I have learned the art of "Blameless
Postmortems." The problem with a Blameless
Postmortem is that it doesn't really work when you're the sole contributor. So this is a blameful
postmortem. And I blame me. (Not the LLM, sorry).
If you saw the website only on August 1, you probably do not understand why I need to write a postmortem
at
all. Everything went swimmingly (ha, ha). But if you had the displeasure of viewing my website between
the hours of 2AM (20 minutes after I went to sleep) and 8AM (when I woke up)
[1]
EST on Aug 3, then you would have seen chaos. Every single username was
transformed to a heinous slur, many unsavory fish had made it into the fishtank, and many beautiful fish
were gone. How did this happen?
The Vulnerabilities
This is not what they changed my username to. I'll let you use your
imagination.
Legacy admin password exposed in data breach:
When creating the website, I used
my childhood username and my childhood 6-digit password for testing. I think the first time it
leaked was on Neopets.com.
[2]
I then set up
Google Auth. From then on, I only logged in with Google Auth. But the password remained. I
simply forgot. This allowed some of the most intelligent and brilliant minds on the internet to
find my password on the Neopets data leak paste, log in as an admin, and approve and disapprove
some really disgusting and horrible fish.
On the plus side, the brilliant minds (while attempting to ban every single user) managed to
accidentally ban themselves. So that vulnerability was only an active issue for an hour or so.
Username update API lacked authentication:
I vibe coded the profile backend,
which allows users to modify their username. I added this feature last minute, figured I'd
review it later, and then didn't. The username modification did not perform any auth logic
whatsoever. whoopsy
JWT not tied to specific user:
There was another security vulnerability - I
used the JWT to authorize login, but never confirmed that the JWT token belonged to the userId /
email associated with it in the admin actions. So you could log in with my username and password,
grab the JWT, and then send that along with your request. While this was a mistake, it ended up
saving me. Fortunately, hackernews user @
iceweaselfan44
used this vulnerability to authorize as an admin and
delete the really bad fish. He was awake, on the other side of the world, removing fish and
helping out.
[3]
The Recovery
Moderation logs. There are so many of these.
I woke up at around 7:45 am, saw a couple pings and messages, and immediately rushed to my desktop.
[4]
Fortunately, I had set up firebase backups.
Unfortunately, I had set them up wrong. I spent a good hour or so diagnosing the errors and then quickly
pushed changes to require authentication.
I had a mod log set up, so undoing the changes was as simple as writing an annoying script that just
undid all the mod actions. Did I learn my lesson about vibe coding? Maybe. I vibe coded the script,
looked over the code, and did a dry run first.
I banned the other mod account ran by IceWeasel
[5]
and
patched the JWT bug - at which point he reached out to me and explained how he created it. We then
hopped on a call and he took a look at the codebase, where he expertly suggested a refactor that would
be more idiomatic with current security practices. And then when I blindly pushed it and it broke
everything, he expertly committed some more changes that fixed it.
Reflection
At this point, you're probably thinking: geeze man. Wow. youve gotta be stupid.
And I'd like to get on my hands and knees and beg for your suspension of belief when I say: yes I am but
not when it comes to my job. It is really fun to just have high velocity, and it is really fun to not do
code reviews and to just push stuff. Sometime

data.title: Customizing tmux
data.author: EPendragon
data.article_summary: 文章主要介绍了终端复用工具 **tmux** 的功能和使用体验。tmux 允许在一个终端中运行多个终端会话，支持创建多个窗口和窗格，便于同时处理多个任务。其主要功能包括保护远程服务器上的运行程序、从不同设备访问远程会话以及灵活的会话管理（如分离和重连）。尽管初始界面不友好且快捷键复杂，但 tmux 高度可定制，用户可以通过编辑 `.tmux.conf` 文件自定义快捷键和外观。例如，更改默认前缀键 `C-b` 为 `C-a`，以及设置分屏和切换窗格的快捷键。文章还提到使用 **iTerm2**、**Powerline10k** 和 **NerdFonts** 可以增强 tmux 的视觉效果。总体而言，tmux 功能强大，但需要一定的学习成本。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：tmux的使用体验和配置方法

不同观点：
• **自定义配置提升使用体验**：[lemonwaterlime] 认为通过取消所有默认键绑定并根据自己的工作流设置键映射，可以让tmux变得非常顺手。他提到这样的配置可以避免误触默认键绑定导致的困扰，并且一旦配置好，tmux就非常稳定，不需要频繁调整。[EPendragon] 也支持这种观点，强调自定义配置可以让tmux更易用和愉悦。

• **默认UI和学习曲线问题**：[akkartik] 认为tmux的默认UI不友好，初学者可能感到不知所措，尤其是需要掌握大量选项和快捷键。尽管可以通过自定义键绑定改善体验，但这并不能完全解决新手面临的入门困难。[aboardRat4] 对此评论带有嘲讽，认为这是典型Mac用户的问题。

• **替代工具**：[benrutter] 推荐Zellij，认为它开箱即用，适合不想过多自定义的人。[linsomniac] 则选择了wezterm，因为它具有更好的原生支持和远程连接功能，但跨平台使用时可能遇到版本兼容性问题。[Jedd] 推荐byobu作为tmux的包装，认为这能接近自定义tmux的体验。[sjbr] 则推荐Oh my tmux! 作为一种配置解决方案。

• **服务器环境中的使用**：[mikepurvis] 关注tmux在服务器环境中作为进程管理器或仪表板的应用，并提出是否会演变成一堆hack以及与其他进程管理工具（如systemd）相比的优劣。[godelski] 强调tmux的主要用途应是远程会话管理，现代终端模拟器已经能很好地处理标签和窗格，因此本地使用tmux没有必要。

补充讨论：
• **配置过程中的技术问题**：[burnt-resistor] 提到tmux配置中一些字符串项不接受外部进程输入，需要使用sed进行模板化处理。
• **编辑器生态的变化**：[alfiedotwtf] 分享了从Vim转向Emacs和Tramp，以及VS Code后，不再需要tmux进行会话管理。

争议焦点：
• tmux的默认UI是否真的"dreadful"（令人畏惧）以及自定义配置是否能显著改善使用体验。
• tmux在现代开发环境中的定位，尤其是在远程会话管理和本地开发场景中的必要性。

44787374.article_content:
I have been exploring some new tools here and there. When I started watching
Primeagen
, I took a note of several tools that he was using and advocating for. One of them was tmux.
What is tmux?
#
tmux
is a terminal multiplexer. What that means is you can have many terminals in one. According to tmux wiki:
tmux is a program which runs in a terminal and allows multiple other terminal programs to be run inside it. Each program inside tmux gets its own terminal managed by tmux, which can be accessed from the single terminal where tmux is running - this called multiplexing and tmux is a terminal multiplexer.
tmux goes further by allowing you to have a lot of control over how the terminals are displayed, how they function, and how are they styled. You can have many separate windows as tabs. You can have many panes within one window. Are you working on several different projects? Then why don’t you have multiple sessions - each of them containing sets of windows and panes - all giving you access to multiple terminals. With a tool like this you no longer need to arrange multiple terminal instance windows on your desktop or using multiple workspaces for those instances - you can have it all in one place.
One additional feature that tmux boasts in is the ability to retain the terminal session upon its closure. Imagine that you have a long running process like a local server or a persistent connection like ssh session. If you were to close that window, you would lose that session and the process that was in it. Tmux has the ability to detach and attach to multiple sessions making them easier to manage and not to worry about losing it.
tmux wiki goes into detail talking about several other features of tmux:
The main uses of tmux are to:
Protect running programs on a remote server from connection drops by running them inside tmux.
Allow programs running on a remote server to be accessed from multiple different local computers.
Work with multiple programs and shells together in one terminal, a bit like a window manager.
For example:
A user connects to a remote server using ssh(1) from an xterm(1) on their work computer and run several programs. perhaps an editor, a compiler and a few shells.
They work with these programs interactively, perhaps start compiling, then close the xterm(1) with tmux and go home for the day.
They are then able to connect to the same remote server from home, attach to tmux, and continue from where they were previously.
My first tmux experience
#
The first impression of tmux didn’t leave me with much excitement of exploring what is truly possible :/ Source:
https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Getting-Started
When I first started using tmux, I felt overwhelmed by the very poor default UI that it offers and the amount of options and shortcuts that I needed to know to operate it well and be productive. It took me several tries before I started to feel more or less comfortable with it.
One of the things that stood out to me right away was how dreadful UI looked. Not only it felt uninviting, but it almost felt “gatekeepy” - if you don’t know how to use it in this configuration, then might as well forget about it. But one thing that kept me going was the promise of a highly customizable terminal that I could make my own at some point.
While promising all of these amazing features, the dreadful tmux UI didn’t necessarily inspire :( Source:
https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Getting-Started
Customization journey
#
To preface, I must mention that I am using
iterm2
with
Powerline10k
and
NerdFonts
. They heavily affect the final look of the tmux due to colors and icons being inherited from the iterm2 configuration. With that said, let’s get into it.
The file that is responsible for customizing tmux - its function and its look - is
.tmux.conf
. This file should be located in user’s Home folder a.k.a.
~/
. That is where tmux will be looking for it.
There are quite a few options when it comes to customizing tmux. One of the first things that I wanted to address was the
prefix
key binding. This prefix is a key combination that you would use to enter the tmux shortcut or command mode. By default, the prefix is
C-b
a.k.a.
Ctrl-b
. One of the common remaps that most people go with is to switch it to
C-a
, which is a lot easier to use. To do that, we need to add the following lines to the configuration file:
# remap prefix from 'C-b' to 'C-a'
unbind C-b
set-option -g prefix C-a
bind-key C-a send-prefix
While researching ways to customize tmux, I stumbled upon several more useful key remaps, which I decided to use:
# split panes using | and -
bind
|
split-window -h
bind
- split-window -v
unbind
'"'
unbind %
# reload config file (change file location to your the tmux.conf you want to use)
bind
r source-file ~/.tmux.conf
;
display-message
"~/.tmux.conf reloaded."
# switch panes using Alt-arrow without prefix
bind
-n M-Left
select
-pane -L
bind
-n M-Right
select
-pane -R
bind
-n M-Up
select
-pane -U
bind
-n M-Down
select

data.title: Show HN: Mathpad – Physical keypad for typing math symbols
data.author: MagneLauritzen
data.article_summary: Mathpad是一款专为简化数学符号输入而设计的键盘，解决了输入数学符号繁琐的问题。它配备了120个数学符号和希腊字母，支持LaTeX、Microsoft Office和LibreOffice等多种输出格式，适用于Windows、macOS和Linux系统。Mathpad采用Gateron KS-33热插拔机械开关，整个设备开源且可定制。项目已完成开发，正在众筹中，计划在活动结束后开始生产并交付。需要注意的是，它仅支持拉丁字母键盘布局，且在Windows系统上需要运行一个小应用程序。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：定制键盘和键帽用于输入特殊符号的优缺点，以及硬件与软件解决方案的比较。

不同观点：
• RossBencina认为，理想情况下应通过多层键盘映射实现无需离开键盘的输入方式。他建议在键盘上增加用于切换层的小型按钮，并强调共享和学习多层映射的重要性。
• throwaway81523质疑高价定制键帽的必要性，提出使用软件工具（如detexify）解决符号查找问题，并认为物理键并非必须。
• eviks指出，硬件解决方案在查找符号时不如软件便捷，建议使用软件显示可搜索的符号表，并可通过现有大键盘进行符号映射。
• darthoctopus分享了使用.XCompose文件进行符号输入的经验，认为这种方法在配置后非常有效，并表示不愿回到没有此功能的机器上工作。
• zokier认为QMK固件的Unicode输入功能不够稳定，且配置繁琐，建议通过QMK键盘自定义符号层，并指出140美元可以购买完整键盘。
• staplung对项目表示赞赏，并询问如何通过shift键组合输入希腊字母大写符号。
• toomuchtodo对项目表示支持，建议考虑使用Elgato Stream Deck作为可编程控制面板。
• tonetegeatinst对项目表示赞赏，并表示在需要时会购买。
• olejorgenb对使用交错布局提出疑问，认为尽管人们习惯于此，但数字键盘并不交错且易于使用。
• threatofrain认为软件搜索界面在符号输入上更具认知优势。
• westurner质疑Mathpad相对于创建每文档符号表和使用Unicode或LaTeX值的效率提升。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点在于硬件键盘与软件解决方案的便捷性和实用性。
• 多层键盘映射的共享、学习和配置被认为是提升输入效率的关键。
• 不同用户对物理键和软件工具的偏好各异，取决于个人使用习惯和需求。
• 价格和配置复杂性也是用户考虑的重要因素。

Mathpad
is a specialized keypad that makes typing mathematical equations as simple as typing regular text. With over
100 mathematical symbols
at your fingertips, this compact and powerful device eliminates the frustration and inefficiency of typing math on a computer.
What if Mathematical Symbols Were as Easy to Type as Regular Letters?
After 3 years of development, Mathpad finally makes this dream a reality. Anyone who’s struggled to type equations knows the pain: When you need symbols beyond basic arithmetic, you’re forced to hunt for them—copy-pasting from the web, digging through clunky symbol pickers, or memorizing obscure alt-codes. Mathpad fixes this. Just press a key, and the symbol appears instantly.
Works Anywhere You Type
Mathpad is designed to be compatible with nearly every platform and environment where you can type text. Whether you’re writing a lab report in
Microsoft Word
, formatting a paper in
LaTeX
, chatting on
Discord
, or documenting code in
VSCode
, Mathpad seamlessly integrates into your workflow.
Its broad compatibility across
Windows, macOS, and Linux
makes it the perfect tool for students writing lab reports, educators creating lesson plans, scientists documenting research, and engineers solving real-world problems.
Outputs for LaTeX and Equation Editors
Mathpad is optimized for both
students and professionals
and supports output for common typesetters and editors. With the press of a key, you can switch between output modes:
Plaintext symbols for universal communication
LaTeX codes for academic writing
Microsoft Office Equation Editor symbols
LibreOffice Equation Editor codes
Whether you’re a student finishing homework or a researcher publishing your newest work, Mathpad has got your back.
Fully Open Source and Customizable
Mathpad is
fully open source
, both hardware and software. Missing a symbol you use daily? No problem! Our
comprehensive documentation
walks you through adding your own symbols - from simple copy-paste customizations to advanced firmware modifications. Mathpad’s firmware is built on
QMK
, the world-class input device firmware library used by keyboard enthusiasts worldwide.
Want to swap mechanical switches? You can—Mathpad uses
hot-swappable Gateron KS-33 switches
.
Features & Specifications
Mathpad gives you direct access to
120 mathematical symbols and Greek letters
, including:
Greek letters
: Complete uppercase and lowercase alphabet
Comparison
: Inequality, approximation, proportionality
Calculus
: Summation, integrals, roots, derivatives
Set theory
: Union, intersection, membership relations
Logic
: Implications, quantifiers, logical operations
Accents
: Superscripts, subscripts, overbars, hats, tilde, dots
Output Modes
:
Plaintext
LaTeX
Microsoft Office Equation Editor
LibreOffice Equation Editor
Specifications
:
Body
: Solid anodized aluminum
Dimensions
: 10 × 7.5 cm (4 × 3 in)
Connectivity
: USB Type-C
Compatibility
: Windows, macOS, Linux
Switches
: Gateron KS-33, hot-swappable
Support & Documentation
Source code and design files
Getting started guide
Online documentation
Discussion forum
Manufacturing Plan
Mathpad isn’t just a concept—it’s fully developed and ready for production. Here’s exactly how we’ll get it to you:
After the campaign ends, off-the-shelf components such as
screws, rubber feet, and key switches
will be ordered. Production orders will be placed for the three custom components: the
PCB
,
anodized aluminum case
, and
custom keycaps
.
Once received, every part will be visually inspected. Devices will then be
assembled, programmed, tested, and packaged
—each with a thank-you note for our backers.
Fulfillment & Shipping
After our production run is complete, we will box everything up and send it along to Crowd Supply’s fulfillment partner, Mouser Electronics, who will handle distribution to backers worldwide. You can learn more about Crowd Supply’s fulfillment service under
Ordering, Paying, and Shipping
in their guide.
Risks & Challenges
We believe in complete transparency. Here’s what you need to know:
User Risks
1. Keyboard Layout Limitation:
Mathpad works only on
Latin-based keyboard layouts
like QWERTY, AZERTY, and DVORAK. It does
not
support non-Latin layouts (e.g., Greek, Russian, Korean, Chinese). This limitation is hardware-based and cannot be avoided. You can find every supported layout in the
documentation
.
2. Windows Software Requirement:
Mathpad requires a small application to be running on
Windows
. This may be an issue for users on strictly managed systems. Read more about this limitation

data.title: Every visual workflow tool is just Excel for developers who gave up
data.author: dalibenothmen
data.article_summary: 文章主要批评了视觉工作流工具（如Zapier、Microsoft Power Automate等）实质上是“放弃开发的开发者的Excel”。这些工具看似简化了复杂逻辑的构建，但实际上创造了难以调试的依赖网络，使问题更难解决。作者指出，这些工具的成功并非因为它们更优秀，而是因为开发者变得懒惰和害怕，产生了自我怀疑，并试图避免做大量决策。此外，这些工具通过订阅模式限制用户能力，收取高额费用，使用户在经济和功能上受限。作者呼吁开发者重新审视这些工具的真实价值，并质疑为 inferior 工具付费的合理性。

A man looking at the window and thinking
Every Visual Workflow Tool is Just Excel for Developers Who Gave Up
Mohamed Ali Ben Othmen
5 min read
·
3 hours ago
--
Listen
Share
There’s a saying that goes “when all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail.” But what happens when you trade your hammer for a Fisher-Price toy hammer and convince yourself it’s an upgrade? That’s exactly what’s happening with visual workflow tools, and I’m tired of pretending it’s not insane.
Every visual workflow tool like Zapier, Microsoft Power Automate, make.com, whatever flavor-of-the-month platform you’re using is just Excel for developers who’ve given up on being developers. And just like Excel, they’re creating a special kind of hell that someone else (probably you, six months from now) will have to deal with.
The Excel Comparison Isn’t an Insult, It’s a Warning
Think about it. Excel and visual workflow tools are fundamentally the same: point-and-click interfaces that let people build complex logic without understanding what they’re actually building. Excel uses cells and formulas, visual workflows use boxes and connectors, but the principle is identical. Both promise to make hard things easy. Both create dependency webs that become absolute nightmares to debug. Both give dangerous amounts of power to people who have no idea what they’re unleashing.
You know what happens with Excel. Karen from accounting builds a “simple” spreadsheet to track expenses. Six months later, it’s a 47-sheet monster with circular references and VLOOKUP formulas that would make a mathematician weep. The company depends on it, nobody understands it, and when it breaks (not if, when), guess who gets called to fix it?
Visual workflows are the same story, just with more colorful boxes and higher monthly fees.
The Question That Should Keep You Up at Night
Here’s what I don’t understand: why are developers whose literal job is to write, understand, and debug code are willingly trading their superpower for drag-and-drop boxes?
Code is infinitely more powerful. You can version control it, test it, refactor it, and when something breaks, you get actual error messages instead of “Node 47 failed.” You can build exactly what you need, scale it however you want, and integrate it with literally anything that has an API.
So why are we choosing tools that are objectively worse at being code? Why are we paying money to make ourselves less capable?
The Uncomfortable Truths We Don’t Want to Admit
Let’s be honest about what’s really happening here. Visual workflow tools aren’t succeeding because they’re better, they’re succeeding because we’ve gotten lazy and scared.
We’ve developed imposter syndrome about our own job.
Somewhere along the way, we started thinking “maybe I’m not smart enough for ‘real’ coding.” So we reach for tools that feel easier, that don’t require us to think through proper architecture or handle edge cases.
We’re suffering from decision fatigue.
Writing code means making a thousand tiny decisions. What framework? How do I structure this? What about error handling? Visual tools reduce those choices, which feels relief until you realize you’ve also reduced your power to actually solve problems.
We’ve bought into the illusion of speed.
“Look, I can build this workflow in 5 minutes!” we say, conveniently ignoring the 5 hours we’ll spend next month trying to figure out why it randomly stopped working.
Management pressure is real.
“Can’t you just use that no-code thing so Sarah from marketing can help maintain it?” Sure, let’s give Sarah the ability to accidentally bring down our entire customer onboarding process. What could go wrong?
But the biggest truth?
We’ve gotten cognitively lazy.
Dragging boxes around feels easier than thinking through the actual problem. It’s the programming equivalent of ordering takeout every night instead of learning to cook.
The Economics Make No Sense
Here’s the part that really gets me: you’re paying premium prices for inferior tools when you literally have the skills to build better solutions for free.
You can write Python, JavaScript, or whatever language you prefer for exactly $0 and have unlimited power. Or you can pay $50+ per month to drag boxes around with artificial constraints. How does this make sense?
These platforms have you trapped in subscription models where you’re paying monthly to be locked into their limited vision of what your workflow should look like. Want to use a custom API? That’s the Enterprise plan for $500/month. Need more than 1000 operations? Upgrade time! Hit a rate limit because too many people are using their shared infrastructure? Sorry, that’s just how it works.
You’re literally paying companies to make you less capable than you naturally are. It’s like a chef paying someone to only let them use a microwave.
The Red Flags You’re Choosing to Ignore
The signs are everywhere, but we keep pretending they’re not deal-breakers:
Vendor lock-in

data.title: 1981 BASIC adventure game comes to a new platform, the TRS-80 MC-10
data.author: vontzy
data.article_summary: 《Arctic Adventure》是一款1981年由Harry McCracken创作的冒险游戏，最初在Radio Shack的TRS-80平台上发布，并收录于《Captain 80's Book of BASIC Adventures》一书中。由于游戏存在严重bug且被遗忘，McCracken在40年后对其进行了修复和改进，使其能在浏览器中运行。游戏修复后获得广泛关注，之后被Jim Gerrie移植到TRS-80 MC-10平台。MC-10是Radio Shack于1983年推出的廉价微型计算机，市场寿命短暂，但因其彩色图形功能而在复古技术圈中受到关注。McCracken对游戏的更新和移植使其从被遗忘的角落重获新生。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：MC-10电脑的历史、使用体验及其在市场上的失败原因

不同观点：
• **simmons的观点**：从个人经历出发，认为MC-10是其第一台电脑，虽然因内存不足导致无法运行复杂程序（如"out of memory"错误），但仍对其童年有积极影响。他提到自己曾熬夜输入冒险游戏程序，尽管最终因内存不足未能运行。这一评论强调了MC-10的局限性和个人体验。

• **anthk的观点**：从技术角度提出解决方案，建议将旧程序改编为现代平台如Inform6或ZMachine，以适应当前技术环境。这表明他关注的是如何让旧程序在新系统上运行，侧重技术适应性。

• **TMWNN的观点**：分析MC-10市场失败的原因，指出MC-10原本是针对低价电脑市场推出的，但因美国人有更多消费能力，且Commodore通过降低VIC-20价格成功抢占市场，导致MC-10未能获得成功。此外，提到Commodore在策略上的自我竞争（如Commodore 16和VIC-20的价格战），进一步削弱了MC-10的市场竞争力。该评论侧重历史背景和市场分析。

补充讨论：
• **争议焦点**：MC-10失败的主要原因。TMWNN认为市场竞争和价格战是关键，而simmons的个人体验则突显了MC-10在技术上的局限性（如内存问题），这可能是其不受欢迎的原因之一。

• **技术细节**：simmons提到的"out of memory"错误，以及anthk提出的改编方案，都指向了MC-10在技术上的局限性及其可能的现代解决方案。

• **历史背景**：TMWNN提供了详细的市场背景分析，涉及多个竞争产品如ZX81、VIC-20和TI 99/4A，并分析了Commodore的战略如何影响MC-10的命运。

总结来看，评论主要围绕MC-10的个人使用体验、技术局限性以及市场失败原因展开，涉及个人回忆、技术建议和市场分析等多个方面。

44787053.article_content:
ARCTIC ADVENTURE FOR THE TRS-80 MC-10
A 1981 ADVENTURE GAME, FINALLY AVAILABLE ON A NEW OLD PLATFORM
GAME BY HARRY MCCRACKEN
PORTED TO THE MC-10 BY JIM GERRIE
Below you will find a playable version of ARCTIC ADVENTURE that works right in your browser, as long as you have a physical keyboard. Type RUN and press return to get started. (If you have any issues, make sure to wait a couple of seconds for it to fully load before typing.)
Scroll down to learn more about this sparkling new version of an ancient game-running, for the first time ever, as far as I know, on Radio Shack's TRS-80 MC-10 platform. In color, even. Or at least with a green background.
Your browser is not supported.
Reset
If you want to know the whole ARCTIC ADVENTURE saga,
head here
. The shortish version is that I wrote the original version in Level II BASIC for the Radio Shack TRS-80 when I was a high school student in love with the text adventures written by the great
Scott Adams
. (No, not that one.) I modeled it closely on Adams' games and--unburdened by petty matters such as realism and scientific accuracy--didn't bother to do any research about the setting. I knew it was cold and polar bears lived there, and that was about it.
My game was published in a 1981 book of type-in adventures called CAPTAIN 80'S BOOK OF BASIC ADVENTURES. I got paid. But I didn't bother to save my creation, and the editor never got around to giving me a copy of the tome. To make matters worse, one of his associates told me that the printed version had a bug that rendered it unwinnable. Within a couple of years, I had given up on trying to write games for public consumption, in part because my writing career was going much better (and still is).
Forty years later, I sought redemption. After acquiring a copy of the CAPTAIN 80 book, I finally got around to typing in the game--and discovered that 1981 glitch was so catastrophic that ARCTIC ADVENTURE wasn't just unwinnable, but unplayable. As long as I was repairing it, I also made some meatier improvements to the gameplay, and figured out how to make my remastered edition run in a web browser--no TRS-80 required.
To my shock, my long-delayed update got a ton of
attention from the gaming press and various nerdy online destinations
. Soon I heard from numerous folks who were playing it, some of whom reported additional bugs or made suggestions for further refinements. ARCTIC ADVENTURE had gone from being broken and forgotten to celebrated--at least for Andy Warhol's requisite 20 minutes.
Since releasing the game on the web, I've heard from several people expressing interest in translating it for other computing platforms. But the first new edition I've seen is
Jim Gerrie
's port for the TRS-80 Model MC-10, a dirt-cheap, late-era TRS-80 I wasn't too familiar with. (By the time of its release, I had mostly moved on to an Atari 400 computer.)
Radio Shack's TRS-80 MC-10, in a catalog shot.
The MC-10 was introduced in 1983 and lasted only a year on the market. At $120, it was designed to compete with the most bargain-basement  of the era's microcomputers. About the size of a hardcover novel, it had a questionable keyboard, only 4KB of RAM, and a limited feature set. Unlike all the TRS-80s I used, however, it offered color graphics, courtesy of a TV you provided yourself.
80 MICRO's
reviewer
said that beginners would quickly outgrow the MC-10. Looking on the bright side, he also noted that people who bought one and concluded they weren't interested in computers after all wouldn't be out much money. By 1983, the market for super-spartan home computers of this type was dwindling. In 1984, the Shack knocked the MC-10's price down to $80. And then it was gone.
Moebius's cover for the Alice ("a marvel of simplicity") manual.
In a fascinating side note, Tandy did strike a deal to release a version of the MC-10 in France, where it was known as the Matra Alice. It was the same machine, but in a striking red case and with a manual illustrated by French cartooning legend
Moebius
. That gave it a veneer of coolness that no Radio Shack product ever offered.
Like many vintage microcomputers, the MC-10 has had a lively afterlife as fodder for 21st century tech historians and tinkerers. Jim Gerrie has written numerous
original MC-10 games
as well as
adapting vintage ones
such as ARCTIC ADVENTURE
. Mike Tinnes created the
JavaScript MC-10 emulator
I used to install Jim's version of the game on this page. I also found James Tamers's
MC-10 emulator for Windows
helpful. And there's a reasonably active
MC-10 group on Facebook
.
Meanwhile, the Alice retains a following of its own--last week, I saw one on display amongst all the Apple IIs, Commodore 64s, Ataris, Amigas, and other bigger-name micros at the Vintage Computer Festival here in the Bay Area.
Jim did a great job of getting ARCTIC ADVENTURE up and running on the MC-10. I see some of my original coding techniques under the hood, but it's a substantial rewrite. It runs quickly--an accomp

• joeld42 认为，只谈论已经完成的部分，而不是计划或目标，能激励自己继续推进项目。这种方法帮助他避免因为提前获得成就感而减少实际工作动力。
• PaulHoule 分享了自己同时推进多个项目的方法，包括处理大量照片和开发自动化工具，尽管任务繁重，但感觉项目进展顺利。
• eawgewag 强调，明确项目的目标和范围至关重要，避免因过多不相关的愿望而使项目变得混乱。
• vouaobrasil 建议减少上网时间，使用有限的工具集，并且不执着于项目，如果项目不合适就果断放弃。
• majora2007 每天坚持工作于自己的开源项目和个人工具，通过 kanban 板跟踪工作，并在处理复杂问题时获得乐趣。
• ahmeneeroe-v2 认为 side projects 只是为了放松，不必感到必须完成，因为主要精力要放在有收入的工作上。
• rozenmd 提出了“两小时内交付”的方法，通过削减范围确保项目在任何时刻都能使用，即使功能不全。
• z_open 认为可以接受项目以未完成或有缺陷的状态结束，只要记录下问题即可。
• add-sub-mul-div 提到使用药物 Bupropion 帮助自己保持对项目的专注和持续输出。
• dmitrygr 限制自己同时只进行两个项目，新项目必须等到现有项目完成或放弃后才能开始。
• jasonvorhe 简单提到“Vibe coding”（凭感觉编码），暗示一种更随性和直觉的项目工作方式。

补充讨论：
- 讨论中涉及多个项目管理策略，包括限制项目数量、明确项目范围、设定短时间内的交付目标等。
- 关于项目完成的态度存在争议：一些人强调必须完成（如 vouaobrasil 的“不执着”和 joeld42 的“完成部分”），而另一些人则认为可以接受项目以不完美状态结束（如 z_open）。
- 不同的工具和方法也被讨论，如 kanban 板（majora2007）和自动化工具（PaulHoule），这些工具帮助管理项目进度和减少工作负担。
- 有人提到通过药物（add-sub-mul-div）或其他个人习惯（vouaobrasil 的减少上网时间）来提高专注力和生产力。

data.title: Tesla withheld data, lied, misdirected police to avoid blame in Autopilot crash
data.author: Hamuko
data.article_summary: 特斯拉在一桩涉及Autopilot的致死车祸案件中被发现隐瞒数据、撒谎并误导警方和原告。在该案件中，特斯拉被部分判定对事故负有责任。审判记录显示，特斯拉隐瞒了关键的碰撞快照数据，这些数据在事故发生后几分钟内就被上传到特斯拉服务器并删除本地副本。特斯拉多年来拒绝承认这些数据的存在，尽管警方和原告多次要求获取。此外，特斯拉律师还指导警方如何撰写数据请求信，以避免提供完整的碰撞数据。特斯拉的这些行为旨在将责任完全推给司机，掩盖Autopilot在事故中的问题。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Tesla在一次自动驾驶相关事故中的数据处理及其责任问题

不同观点：
• Ajedi32：认为Tesla没有将事故数据提供给调查人员是不可辩护的，尤其是在他们自己保留数据用于分析的情况下。尽管事故本身是由于司机超速和不当使用自动驾驶功能导致的，与Tesla无关，但Tesla拒绝提供数据显得像是无能，而非恶意。

• elAhmo：认为只要没有对不当使用自动驾驶的行为追究刑事责任，现状就不会改变。对于Tesla这样的大公司来说，罚款只是九牛一毛，不具威慑力。

• goosejuice：认为Tesla在此事件中的行为很愚蠢，但事故责任明显在于司机。自动辅助驾驶本质上只是巡航控制，Tesla已经在系统中提供了足够的警告。他觉得Tesla在此案中受到了不公平的对待，并怀疑存在政治偏见。

• throwanem：对Tesla自动删除车载数据快照的决策表示质疑，希望了解这一决定是如何被合理化的。

• declan_roberts：对文章中术语混用感到困惑，想明确在事故中是完全自动驾驶（FSD）还是自动转向（autosteer）功能在运作。同时指出，Tesla提供了事故中的遥测数据，这本身是难得的。

• sbassi：认为调查人员的失误也是调查失败的原因之一，暗示Tesla并非唯一责任方。

• duxup：认为Tesla的行为规模之大，应该构成刑事犯罪。

• 0cf8612b2e1e：对AI生成的标题图片感到厌烦，认为这种做法降低了文章的可信度。

• steveBK123：认为在自动驾驶技术的发展中，部分公司试图等待监管松动，而不是真正提升技术水平，以此来达到安全标准。

• hn_throwaway_99：同样对AI生成的图片感到不满，认为这种做法让文章显得不专业，可能会让人更倾向于忽视文章内容。

• buyucu：认为Tesla长期以来一直是这样操作的，暗示这是公司一贯的策略。

• ChrisArchitect：提到相关案件，Tesla被要求支付部分因自动驾驶事故导致的赔偿金。

• dotcoma：简单表示对此事的困惑。

补充讨论：
• 争议的焦点在于Tesla是否应向调查人员提供事故数据，以及其拒绝提供数据的行为是出于无能还是故意。
• 部分评论者认为Tesla在此事件中受到了不公平的对待，自动驾驶功能本身的警告和使用限制已经非常明确。
• 对AI生成图片的讨论虽然偏离主题，但也反映出读者对文章呈现方式的关注。

44787780.article_content:
Tesla
Tesla withheld data, lied, and misdirected police and plaintiffs to avoid blame in Autopilot crash
Fred Lambert
| Aug 4 2025 - 8:54 am PT
45 Comments
Tesla was caught withholding data, lying about it, and misdirecting authorities in the wrongful death case involving Autopilot that it lost this week.
The automaker was undeniably covering up for Autopilot.
Last week, a jury found Tesla partially liable for a wrongful death involving a crash on Autopilot. I explained the case in the verdict in
this article
and
video
.
But we now have access to the trial transcripts, which confirm that Tesla was extremely misleading in its attempt to place all the blame on the driver.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The company went as far as to actively withhold critical evidence that explained Autopilot’s performance around the crash.
Tesla
withheld the crash‑snapshot data that its own server received within minutes of the collision
Within about three minutes of the crash, the Model S uploaded a “collision snapshot”—video, CAN‑bus streams, EDR data, etc.—to Tesla’s servers, the “Mothership”, and received an acknowledgement. The vehicle then deleted its local copy, resulting in Tesla being the only entity having access.
What ensued were years of battle to get Tesla to acknowledge that this collision snapshot exists and is relevant to the case.
The police repeatedly attempted to obtain the data from the collision snapshot, but Tesla led the authorities and the plaintiffs on a lengthy journey of deception and misdirection that spanned years.
Here, in chronological order, is what happened based on all the evidence in the trial transcript:
1 | 25 Apr 2019 – The crash and an instant upload Tesla pretended never happened
Within ~3 minutes of the cras
h, the Model S packaged sensor video, CAN‑bus, EDR, and other streams into a single “snapshot_collision_airbag-deployment.tar” file and pushed it to Tesla’s server, then deleted its local copy.
We know that now, thanks to forensic evidence extracted from the onboard computer.
The plaintiffs hired Alan Moore, a mechanical engineer who specializes in accident reconstruction, to forensically recover data from the Autopilot ECU (computer).
Based on the data, Moore was able to confirm that Tesla had this “collision snapshot” all along, but “unlinked” it from the vehicle:
“That tells me within minutes of this crash Tesla had all of this data … the car received an acknowledgement … then said ‘OK, I’m done, I’m going to unlink it.’”
The plaintiffs tried to obtain this data, but Tesla told them that it didn’t exist.
Tesla’s written discovery responses were shown during the trial to prove that the company acted as if this data were not available.
2 | 23 May 2019 – Tesla’s lawyer scripts the homicide investigator’s evidence request
Corporal Riso, a homicide investigator with the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP), sought Tesla’s help in retrieving telemetry data to aid in reconstructing the crash.
He was put in contact with Tesla attorney Ryan McCarthy and asked if he needed to subpoena Tesla to get the crash data.
Riso said of McCarthy during the trial:
“He said it’s not necessary.
‘Write me a letter and I’ll tell you what to put in the letter.’
”
At the time, he didn’t see Tesla as an adversary in this case and thought that McCarthy would facilitate the retrieval of the data without having to go through a formal process. However, the lawyer crafted the letter to avoid sending the police the full crash data.
Riso followed the instructions verbatim. He said during the trial:
“I specifically wrote down what the attorney at Tesla told me to write down in the letter.”
But McCarthy specifically crafted the letter to ommit sharing the colllision snapshot, which includes bundled video, EDR, CAN bus, and Autopilot data.
Instead, Tesla provided the police with infotainment data with call logs, a copy of the Owner’s Manual, but not the actual crash telemetry from the Autopilot ECU.
Tesla never said that it already had this data for more than a month by now.
3 | June 2019 – A staged “co‑operation” that corrupts evidence
Tesla got even more deceptice when the police specifically tried to collect the data directly from the Autopilot computer.
On June 19, 2019, Riso physically removed the MCU and Autopilot ECU from the Tesla.
Again, the investigator thought that Tesla was being collaborative with the investigation at the time so he asked the company how to get the data out of the computer. He said at the trial:
I had contacted Mr. McCarthy and asked him how I can get this data off of the computer components. He said that he would coordinate me meeting with a technician at their service center, the Tesla service center in Coral Gables.
Tesla arranged for Riso to meet Michael Calafell, a Tesla technician, at the local service center in in Coral Gables with the Autopilot ECU and the Model S’ MCU, the two main onboard computers.
To be clear, Tesla already had all this data in its servers and could have jus

data.title: Qwen Image
data.author: error404x
data.article_summary: Qwen-Image是一款由Qwen系列推出的图像生成基础模型，在复杂文本渲染和精准图像编辑方面取得了显著进展。该模型在文本生成和编辑上表现优异，尤其对中文文本渲染效果极佳。它支持多种艺术风格的图像生成，并能够进行高级图像编辑操作，如风格迁移、对象插入或删除、细节增强及文本编辑。此外，Qwen-Image还具备图像理解能力，支持对象检测、语义分割、深度估计等任务。该模型已在Hugging Face和ModelScope上发布，并采用Apache 2.0许可协议。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：关于Qwen图像处理模型的功能和影响的讨论

不同观点：
• [积极评价功能] **nickandbro** 认为Qwen模型的优点在于它只会对需要编辑的元素应用AI修改，而不会像4o图像生成模型那样改变无关部分（如人脸）。这表明Qwen在细节处理上更精准。

• [关注特定应用] **yjftsjthsd-h** 特别提到Qwen模型的文本生成和编辑能力非常出色，尤其是文本部分非常突出。这表明该模型在处理文字方面有独特的优势。

• [对中国开源模型的乐观态度] **artninja1988** 表示对中国开源模型频繁发布的乐观态度，认为这些模型的发布带来了希望，可能推动行业进步。

• [对普及速度的担忧] **anon191928** 指出尽管这些模型功能强大，但普及可能需要数年时间。此外，提到Adobe并不是唯一在这一领域竞争的公司，暗示市场竞争激烈。

• [技术细节的关注] **djoldman** 关注Qwen模型的技术文档，特别是数据过滤部分（3.2节），表明讨论已经深入到技术实现的细节层面。

补充讨论：
• 评论中不仅包含对模型功能的直接评价，还涉及对模型应用前景的讨论，以及对开源模型生态的期待。
• 技术文档和具体实现细节（如数据过滤）也成为了讨论的一部分，说明部分用户对技术的实现方式感兴趣。
• 对Adobe等公司的提及，反映了用户在讨论技术时也考虑到了市场竞争和应用落地的现实因素。

Quick Start
Install the latest version of diffusers
pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers
The following contains a code snippet illustrating how to use the model to generate images based on text prompts:
from
diffusers
import
DiffusionPipeline
import
torch
model_name =
"Qwen/Qwen-Image"
# Load the pipeline
if
torch.cuda.is_available():
torch_dtype = torch.bfloat16
device =
"cuda"
else
:
torch_dtype = torch.float32
device =
"cpu"
pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(model_name, torch_dtype=torch_dtype)
pipe = pipe.to(device)
positive_magic = [
"en"
:
"Ultra HD, 4K, cinematic composition."
# for english prompt,
"zh"
:
"超清，4K，电影级构图"
# for chinese prompt,
]
# Generate image
prompt =
'''A coffee shop entrance features a chalkboard sign reading "Qwen Coffee 😊 $2 per cup," with a neon light beside it displaying "通义千问". Next to it hangs a poster showing a beautiful Chinese woman, and beneath the poster is written "π≈3.1415926-53589793-23846264-33832795-02384197". Ultra HD, 4K, cinematic composition'''
negative_prompt =
" "
# Generate with different aspect ratios
aspect_ratios = {
"1:1"
: (
1328
,
1328
),
"16:9"
: (
1664
,
928
),
"9:16"
: (
928
,
1664
),
"4:3"
: (
1472
,
1140
),
"3:4"
: (
1140
,
1472
)
}
width, height = aspect_ratios[
"16:9"
]
image = pipe(
prompt=prompt + positive_magic[
"en"
],
negative_prompt=negative_prompt,
width=width,
height=height,
num_inference_steps=
50
,
true_cfg_scale=
4.0
,
generator=torch.Generator(device=
"cuda"
).manual_seed(
42
)
).images[
0
]
image.save(
"example.png"
)

One of its standout capabilities is high-fidelity text rendering across diverse images. Whether it’s alphabetic languages like English or logographic scripts like Chinese, Qwen-Image preserves typographic details, layout coherence, and contextual harmony with stunning accuracy. Text isn’t just overlaid—it’s seamlessly integrated into the visual fabric.
Beyond text, Qwen-Image excels at general image generation with support for a wide range of artistic styles. From photorealistic scenes to impressionist paintings, from anime aesthetics to minimalist design, the model adapts fluidly to creative prompts, making it a versatile tool for artists, designers, and storytellers.
When it comes to image editing, Qwen-Image goes far beyond simple adjustments. It enables advanced operations such as style transfer, object insertion or removal, detail enhancement, text editing within images, and even human pose manipulation—all with intuitive input and coherent output. This level of control brings professional-grade editing within reach of everyday users.
But Qwen-Image doesn’t just create or edit—it understands. It supports a suite of image understanding tasks, including object detection, semantic segmentation, depth and edge (Canny) estimation, novel view synthesis, and super-resolution. These capabilities, while technically distinct, can all be seen as specialized forms of intelligent image editing, powered by deep visual comprehension.
Together, these features make Qwen-Image not just a tool for generating pretty pictures, but a comprehensive foundation model for intelligent visual creation and manipulation—where language, layout, and imagery converge.

Microsoft is now a $4 trillion company, but that's cold comfort for all those ex (and soon to be ex) employees who helped make that achievement possible.
Credit:
3rdtimeluckystudio - Shutterstock 2173796959
If you own Microsoft stock, you’ve got to be happy.
Microsoft’s latest financial results for the quarter ending June 30, 2025 were robust: Revenue reached $76.4 billion (up 18% year-over-year), with net income at $27.2 billion (up 24%). The primary driver was robust growth in Microsoft’s cloud and AI businesses. Azure’s revenue, which has finally been separated out in the financial reporting, now stands at $75 billion in annual revenue, representing a 34% surge for the year.
Put it all together, and you can see why Microsoft has joined Nvidia in the $4-trillion valuation club.
So much for the good news. Despite those impressive financials, Microsoft has laid off a substantial number of employees this year — about 25,000, to be exact, including
roughly 9,100 in July alone
(approximately 4% of its workforce). The layoffs have affected a broad range of divisions, including Xbox, engineering, and management layers.
What’s driving these cuts is clearly not poor performance. Instead, Microsoft is betting that its aggressive
$80 billion AI investments will pay off
. Don’t take my word for it:  Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella recently noted
the “incongruence” of laying off employees even as Microsoft is “thriving.”
He called this dynamic “the enigma of success” in a tech industry where progress demands constant change, even when things are going well.
“I want to express my sincere gratitude to those who have left,” he added. “Their contributions have shaped who we are as a company, helping build the foundation we stand on today. And for that, I am deeply grateful.”
I’m sure deep gratitude will help keep a roof over their heads.
Microsoft is far from alone in
dumping once-valued employees
for cheaper AI alternatives.
IBM has cut 8,000
jobs
so far this year. In particular, IBM is gradually replacing clerical jobs with AI, while its AskHR bot has taken over much of HR’s old workloads. At the same time,
Meta is reducing its staff by 5% in 2025
as it switches gears from its metaverse dud to AI.
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy put an even finer point on where things are headed. “As we roll out more generative AI and agents, it should change the way our work is done.” That means, he said, “
We will need fewer people doing some of the jobs
that are being done today.”
This isn’t just happening in the US. In India,
Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) has cut 12,000 jobs this year.
Why? Because its customers are moving to AI, which has sharply cut the outsourcing work the company has historically profited from. Meanwhile, in Japan,
Indeed and Glassdoor’s parent company has laid off 1,300 workers
, approximately 6% of its workforce, according to CEO
Hisayuki “Deko” Idekoba
.
“AI is changing the world,” he said. It certainly changed the world of the 130,000 or so tech jobs that have been lost this year,
according to estimates by The Bridge Chronicle
.
Oh, and by the way, Indeed reports that
tech job postings in July were down 36% from their early 2020 levels
.
Is this a great time to be looking for a tech job or what!? But for every fantasy job, like the
$100-million AI jobs Meta is supposedly offering
, there are hundreds of tech workers who have kissed their six-figure positions goodbye and thousands of clerical staffers who will no longer be making five-figure annual incomes.
There’s one little problem with all these job cuts. We still don’t know whether AI can deliver the work goods. Sure, some jobs, such as repetitive HR or call-center work, can be largely replaced.  Heck, we’ve seen that happen before. I remember when many call-center jobs were located in the US — before companies figured out that outsourcing such jobs to low-cost countries was cheaper. For jobs like these, AI is just the next step in cost-cutting.
Companies often use AI like that — to cut costs. Not many are using it to help good workers become great workers. Instead, CEOs are buying the illusion that AI can magically replace highly skilled workers.
I hate to break it to you: It can’t. Take programming. According to the
2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey
, 84% of programmers now use or plan to use AI tools in their workflow. However — and this is a crucial point —
46% of AI-using developers don’t trust AI results
. In fact, even as AI developer tools have supposedly improved, programmers are trusting them even less.
Why? Because they’re spending a lot of their time fixing AI mistakes. AI programming tools make fine interns, but they’re not senior or even mid-level developers.

44788936.article_content:
On-Prem
7
IT firing spree: Shrinking job market looks even worse after BLS revisions
7
The payroll growth we thought we experienced in May and June? Gone, like tears in the rain
Brandon Vigliarolo
Mon 4 Aug 2025
//
16:42 UTC
The US IT jobs market hasn't exactly been robust thus far in 2025, and downward revisions to May and June's Bureau of Labor Statistics data mean IT jobs lost in July are part of an even deeper sector slowdown than previously believed.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics
reported
relatively flat job growth last month, but unimpressive payroll growth numbers hid an even deeper reason to be worried: Most of the job growth reported (across all employment sectors) in May and June was incorrect.
According to the BLS, May needed to be revised down by 125,000 jobs to just 19,000 added jobs; June had to be revised down by even more, with 133,000 erroneous new jobs added to company payrolls that month. That meant just 14,000 new jobs were added in June.
"Adjustments at those levels of magnitude are not acceptable from any organization," IT management consulting firm Janco said of the May and June modifications. Janco
blamed
the modifications on "poor data capture, poor infrastructure, incompetence, or political gerrymandering," but regardless of the cause, it means that the IT job market is looking decidedly less healthy than it did a month ago.
"According to the latest revised data by the BLS, the IT Job Market shrank by 26,500 YTD," Janco CEO Victor Janulaitis said of the latest data. "That is after adjusting the May data down by 4,300, June data down by 7,800 jobs, and reporting that 10,300 jobs were lost in July."
For those keeping count, that's 20,300 more than the 6,200-job shortfall at the same point in 2024, and we're now in what tends to be the worst half of the year for layoffs.
The current year to date IT jobs market losses compared to 2024 - Click to enlarge
US President Trump
fired
BLS Commissioner Erika McEntarfer shortly after the publication of the report, alleging BLS had rigged the data to make him look weak.
Uncertainty hurts
Janco, which for a long time has relied exclusively on BLS data for its monthly jobs report that focuses on IT employment, said that it plans to diversify its data sources because of the massive revisions.
Against that backdrop, Janco reports that BLS data peg the IT-sector unemployment rate at 5.5 percent in July - well above the national rate of 4.2 percent. Meanwhile, the broader tech occupation unemployment rate was just 2.9 percent, as
reported
by CompTIA.
Former and current Microsofties react to the latest round of layoffs
Laid-off AWS employee describes cuts as 'cold and soulless'
Intel swings the axe again as it looks to lose 5,000 staff
Microsoft kicks off new fiscal year with more layoffs
Janulaitis blamed economic uncertainty for continuing to drag down IT hiring - a sentiment CompTIA agreed on, though the firm noted that there were still some bright spots of demand.
CompTIA stated that, while staffing reductions were made in IT, custom software services, cloud infrastructure and telecom, other roles such as developers and software engineers, system architects, support specialists, and cybersecurity mavens are among those in demand. Janco said that unfilled IT-specific roles tend to be related to AI, LLMs, Blockchain, and OmniCommerce technologies.
For all that uncertainty, CompTIA noted that it did find some solid evidence of job growth in the AI space, though not for AI-exclusive roles, which haven't grown over the past two months. Instead, CompTIA said that roles
with
AI competency are where it's at.
"CompTIA's AI Hiring Index indicates relatively higher growth in hiring demand for the broad range of positions where employers require some type of AI skill to perform effectively in the job role," the certification firm said.
In other words, amid economic instability and AI inflation, landing a good IT job is tougher than ever unless you know how to engineer a good prompt. ®

data.title: AI promised efficiency. Instead, it's making us work harder
data.author: mooreds
data.article_summary: 文章主要讨论了AI工具本应提高工作效率，但实际上却让人们工作得更辛苦。作者指出，尽管AI可以自动化一些任务，但它增加了我们的认知负担，导致更多工作填补了节省出来的时间。研究显示，使用AI工具的开发人员完成任务的时间比不使用时长19%，尽管他们自认为更快。此外，AI的采用与交付效率下降相关。文章强调，AI工具带来了新的认知负荷，人们需要花费精力审核和修正AI生成的内容，这使得深度思考和工作变得更加困难。作者建议，虽然AI工具有其价值，但我们需要更明智地使用，以避免过度消耗和倦怠。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：AI工具对开发者和团队生产力的影响，包括其优缺点和应用场景。

不同观点：
• [Bukhmanizer] 认为AI工具在团队中可能带来隐患，尤其是当开发者不完全理解AI生成的代码时，可能会导致代码库的质量问题。他强调需要适当的流程来规范AI的使用，以避免潜在的风险。

• [vasco] 支持AI工具的使用，特别是对于小型任务和已知问题。他认为AI在处理接近其能力极限的任务时效果不佳，但可以有效处理其擅长的问题。他建议对AI的能力保持清醒认识，避免浪费时间在不适合的任务上。

• [bko] 对AI工具的影响持怀疑态度，指出文章中关于AI提高生产力和导致认知负担的矛盾观点。他认为文章在AI对生产力的影响上立场不一致，并质疑对AI的批评是否源于对技术的不适。

• [pfisherman] 认为AI工具确实提高了生产力和效率，使人们能够在相同时间内完成更多任务。他强调问题的类型会随着技术发展而改变，关键在于适应和解决正确的问题。

• [kebman] 批评AI工具导致更多“管理工具的工作”，如提示工程和输出验证，而非真正的高价值工作。他认为这导致了“生产力剧场”现象，而非实际的生产力提升。

• [firefoxd] 分享了团队中因AI工具使用而导致的实际问题，特别是初级开发者在不完全理解AI生成代码的情况下提交大型PR，增加了团队工作量。他提出通过要求演示来确保开发者理解代码。

• [ctoth] 对AI工具的时间节省效果持保留态度，分享了个人使用AI工具的经历，认为虽然有趣但未必真正节省时间。

• [hintymad] 认为AI带来的工作量增加可能与其他自动化技术相似，不一定是AI独有的问题，可能与企业文化和业务需求有关。

• [amirhirsch] 提到METR研究中的经验丰富的开发者在使用AI工具时获得了巨大的提升，批评博客对该研究的解读有误。

• [snitzr] 认为当前美国经济依赖于AI的炒作，对AI的实际影响持怀疑态度。

• [6gvONxR4sf7o] 从历史角度分析技术进步对工作时间的影响，认为即使效率提高，工作时间并不会因此减少，而是转向更复杂的任务。

• [Oras] 分享了使用AI工具在长期项目中的积极经验，认为AI在设计和规划阶段节省了大量时间，尽管短期内开发速度可能较慢。

• [kachapopopow] 认为AI帮助他完成了之前因懒惰或不重视而未完成的项目，但也指出这可能导致跳过一些必要的设计工作。

• [tcrow] 认为AI在专注于模块化开发和服务规范时效果最佳，强调人类在设计和规范上的责任，AI在开发实现上可以提供有效帮助。

• [nathan_compton] 认为AI在快速启动新项目和协助重构方面非常有用，强调AI并未减少他在软件设计上的思考。

补充讨论：
- 争议的焦点在于AI工具是否真正提高了生产力，或者只是增加了工作复杂性和认知负担。
- 不同观点中对AI工具的使用场景和预期效果存在显著差异，一些评论者强调需要适当的流程和管理以最大化AI的效益。
- 团队中不同开发者对AI工具的理解和使用能力也是讨论的重要方面，初级开发者可能需要更多指导和监督。

AI promised efficiency. Instead, it’s making us work harder.
AI tools were supposed to free up our time—but they’re increasing our cognitive load and making us less productive. Here’s what’s really happening (and how to use them without burning out).
Kelly Vaughn
